newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian army colonel escapes Lagos bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian army colonel escapes Lagos bomb attack.

text.p: An army colonel who is one of the closest aides of Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha narrowly escaped a bomb attack as he was driving along a road in Lagos on Monday, a witness said.

Colonel Muhammed Marwa, the military administrator of Lagos state, was not hurt but the blast seriously injured two men sitting in the last car of the convoy in which he was travelling, Lagos state police commissioner Abubakar Tsav said.
Six suspects had been arrested, Tsav told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN).
"The administrator was not injured, we thank God," he said.
Witnesses said the colonel, who served as Nigeria's defence attache in Washington until August, was clearly the target of the attack but escaped by a whisker.
"The car in which Colonel Marwa was riding had just passed and the vehicle hit was the last in his entourage," said Ibrahim Bello, a communications engineer at the scene.
"The windows of the vehicle were shattered in the back and front," he added.
Tsav said the explosive device, suspected to be a time-bomb, had been placed under a stone and went off as the convoy was passing along the Opebi link road towards the state secretariat nearby.
NAN quoted police deputy superintendent Goni Gogo as saying there was a striking similarity between the device that exploded on Monday and a bomb that killed three people last month.

Three people, including the head of airport security, were killed in a bungled car bomb explosion in Lagos in November. Police said the victims were agents of the exiled opposition leader and Nobel Prize winner for literature, Wole Soyinka.
Marwa is one of the officers closest to Abacha, who took power in 1993 in the crisis unleashed when a previous military leader annulled a presidential poll that would have restored democracy.

After his assignment in Washington, Marwa was in August appointed administrator of Lagos, the bastion of the opposition symbolised by Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll who has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president.
In January Abacha's son died in a plane crash for which a previously unknown group claimed responsibility. Security agencies dismissed the claim.

Since then there has been a string of bomb blasts in Nigeria, some on military premises, and a number of high-profile individuals have been murdered, including Abiola's senior wife who was killed in June.
